article.title: AsyncAPI npm Packages Backdoored via GitHub Actions Token Theft, Exposing Nearly 3 Million Weekly Downloads
article.summary: An attacker exploited a misconfigured GitHub Actions workflow to steal a publishing token and push a remote-access trojan into five AsyncAPI npm package versions.
article.body_markdown:
## Overview

An attacker compromised the open-source AsyncAPI project's npm publishing pipeline on July 14, 2026, pushing a remote-access trojan into five package versions with a combined weekly download footprint of nearly 3 million, according to [Aikido Security](https://www.aikido.dev/blog/asyncapi-npm-packages-backdoored-via-github-actions) and [Socket](https://socket.dev/blog/asyncapi-supply-chain-attack). The attacker gained access by abusing a misconfigured GitHub Actions workflow to steal a publishing token, then let the project's own release pipeline sign and ship the malicious code.

## What We Know

The attack began in the `asyncapi/generator` repository, where a workflow used the `pull_request_target` trigger — a configuration that "runs with access to repository secrets even when the workflow checks out code from an external pull request," [according to Aikido](https://www.aikido.dev/blog/asyncapi-npm-packages-backdoored-via-github-actions). Security researchers call this class of misconfiguration a "pwn request," [per Wiz](https://www.wiz.io/blog/m-red-team-asyncapi-supply-chain-compromise-via-github-actions), because it lets an outside contributor's code run with the base repository's full secret access.

On July 14, the attacker opened 37 pull requests against the generator repository, [Wiz reported](https://www.wiz.io/blog/m-red-team-asyncapi-supply-chain-compromise-via-github-actions). "Almost all attempted to add a fake charity donation page," providing cover while "a single PR exploited a misconfigured GitHub Actions workflow to steal a highly privileged Personal Access Token," [Wiz said](https://www.wiz.io/blog/m-red-team-asyncapi-supply-chain-compromise-via-github-actions). At 05:08 UTC, the attacker opened PR #2155, which "contained obfuscated JavaScript that exfiltrated the npm publish token to `rentry[.]co`," [Aikido found](https://www.aikido.dev/blog/asyncapi-npm-packages-backdoored-via-github-actions).

With the stolen token, the attacker pushed malicious commits and let the project's legitimate GitHub Actions release workflow publish the poisoned packages starting at 07:10 UTC: `@asyncapi/generator@3.3.1`, `@asyncapi/generator-helpers@1.1.1`, and `@asyncapi/generator-components@0.7.1`, [Aikido and Socket both confirmed](https://socket.dev/blog/asyncapi-supply-chain-attack). A second AsyncAPI repository, `asyncapi/spec-json-schemas`, "was compromised 58 minutes later," when commits pushed to its master branch "injected a dropper into `index.js`, triggering `if-nodejs-release.yml` to publish `@asyncapi/specs@6.11.2-alpha.1` and `@asyncapi/specs@6.11.2`," [according to StepSecurity](https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/compromised-next-branch-pushes-malicious-asyncapi-generator-generator-helpers-and-generator-components-to-npm). StepSecurity noted that both intrusions used commits attributed to the same placeholder identity, "Your Name" with the GitHub login `invalid-email-address`, suggesting a single operation across both repositories.

Because the packages were published through AsyncAPI's own legitimate workflow, they "carry valid npm OIDC provenance attestations," [Aikido noted](https://www.aikido.dev/blog/asyncapi-npm-packages-backdoored-via-github-actions) — the cryptographic signal npm uses to vouch for a package's build origin offered no protection here, since the attacker never needed to steal a separate npm credential. Combined, the five malicious versions carried "roughly 2.9 million weekly downloads, with `@asyncapi/specs` alone accounting for around 2.7 million," an identical figure reported independently by [Aikido](https://www.aikido.dev/blog/asyncapi-npm-packages-backdoored-via-github-actions) and [Socket](https://socket.dev/blog/asyncapi-supply-chain-attack).

The malicious code does not rely on npm's install-time hooks at all. Instead, it "fires when the poisoned module is `require()`d during normal use," [StepSecurity explained](https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/compromised-next-branch-pushes-malicious-asyncapi-generator-generator-helpers-and-generator-components-to-npm), spawning a detached process that "fetches an encrypted Node.js loader from IPFS, writes it to disk as `sync.js`, and starts it as a detached process," [Aikido reported](https://www.aikido.dev/blog/asyncapi-npm-packages-backdoored-via-github-actions). GBHackers noted that "this design may help attackers evade protections introduced in npm v12 that block package scripts by default," [GBHackers said](https://gbhackers.com/miasma-worm-returns-as-rat/) — a default [Machine Herald reported](/article/2026-07/13-npm-v12-ships-with-install-scripts-disabled-by-default-after-a-year-of-supply-chain-attacks) npm shipped roughly a year into a wave of supply-chain attacks. On Linux, the final-stage implant persists by writing `~/.config/systemd/user/miasma-monitor.service` and enabling it, [according to Aikido](https://www.aikido.dev/blog/asyncapi-npm-packages-backdoored-via-github-actions), establishing "a persistent implant with a real remote shell."

The malware communicates with its operators "over multiple channels including HTTP, Nostr relays, Ethereum smart contracts, and a libp2p mesh network," [Wiz found](https://www.wiz.io/blog/m-red-team-asyncapi-supply-chain-compromise-via-github-actions), though Socket's analysis concluded that "HTTP on port 8080 is the only real beacon and command channel" in practice, connecting back to a single server. Its runtime code "explicitly self-identifies as `M-RED-TEAM v6.4`" in internal comments, both [Wiz](https://www.wiz.io/blog/m-red-team-asyncapi-supply-chain-compromise-via-github-actions) and [Socket](https://socket.dev/blog/asyncapi-supply-chain-attack) independently confirmed. Researchers have not tied the operation to a named threat actor: "At this time, we are not making any definitive attribution," [Wiz said](https://www.wiz.io/blog/m-red-team-asyncapi-supply-chain-compromise-via-github-actions).

All five malicious versions have since been removed from the registry, and StepSecurity advised developers to delete lockfiles and reinstall from the last known-clean releases, such as `@asyncapi/generator@3.3.0`.

## What We Don't Know

No threat actor has been formally named, and researchers have explicitly declined to attribute the operation. It also remains unclear how many downstream projects actually executed the malicious code before the packages were pulled, as opposed to simply downloading them without triggering the `require()`-time payload.

## Analysis

The attack illustrates a gap that npm's recent hardening efforts don't close. npm's decision to disable install scripts by default was built to stop the most common supply-chain pattern — malicious code that runs the moment `npm install` executes. This payload sidesteps that defense entirely by waiting until the library is actually imported, and it reached the registry through the project's own trusted, cryptographically attested release pipeline rather than a stolen npm token. That combination — a legitimate CI/CD workflow doing the attacker's publishing, wrapped in a provenance attestation that vouches only for the build process and not the code's intent — is a harder problem for registry-level defenses to catch than a compromised maintainer account.
